sections.text: Arjuna said: My Lord! Thy words concerning the Supreme Secret of Self, given for my blessing, have dispelled the illusions which surrounded me.
भवाप्ययौ हि भूतानां श्रुतौ विस्तरशो मया।
O Lord, whose eyes are like the lotus petal! Thou hast described in detail the origin and the dissolution of being, and Thine own Eternal Majesty.
I believe all as Thou hast declared it. I long now to have a vision of thy Divine Form, O Thou Most High!

We have started discussing Chapter 11, Vishwarupadarshan, the Vision of the Cosmic Form. Up till now in Bhagavad Gita, we have learned that all of us are trying to liberate ourselves from our sorrows. In the very first chapter, we defined our condition.
From my perspective, life is full of sorrows and joys, but they dont come as cleanly defined as we would like them to be. Sorrows come with a little joy, and joys come with a little sorrow. Everything that is positive comes with a little negative, and everything negative has some positive in it.
The very first chapter defined our condition. To get out of this, we are trying all our means to overcome these limitations. In the first five chapters, we define who we are and from what perspective we are seeing our life, and therefore why we have these limitations.
We have seen that we are defining ourselves by our accomplishments, our relationships, our abilities, and also our limitations. From that perspective, when I see the world, Im a minuscule being and the world is out there to get me. The vast world out there is the karma Falada -- the field of my activity -- and I have very limited control over what comes out of my actions.
In that situation, I constantly try to find what is right and what is wrong, what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, but I cant find a clear definition. From chapter two onwards, we have seen why that perspective is not correct. That perspective -- me looking at myself from a very narrow angle -- is creating all this confusion.
If I change the perspective about who I am, which Bhagavan clarifies in chapter two, I learn that you are not who you think you are. This mortal self is not you but your equipment. My body, my mind, my intellect -- these are my equipment, but not me.
I consider them to be me and associate all their limitations as my limitations. Up to chapter five, we learned what that equipment is all about and how using it in this world effectively will get me to where I want to be, which is a state of complete bliss. Then we learned the art of meditation in chapter six -- how to meditate upon that other self which I have not experienced yet, but which is my real self.
So the quest from chapter 7 onward is to define that self -- the self which I have not yet identified with, but identification with which will end all my sorrows and limitations. We have learned that that self is the Almighty, all-pervading self. That self is none other than the self which I consider to be myself, the one self which constantly reminds me that I exist.
That self is the same self as the self outside. But the change of perspective is what I need. So how do I get to that was the topic of chapter 10.
How do I now start identifying with that higher self? By seeing that self in everything and every being. In chapter 10, the Vibhuti yoga, Yoga of Divine Glories, we have learned that Bhagavan says there anything glorious, splendid, powerful, wonderful, you see in this world. Consider that is that because of me, the self in it.
So the theme of chapter 10 was that I am the origin and dissolution of all the being. Aham Sarvasya prabhavaha matthaha Sarva Prabhartate. When you take that statement -- that everything is pervaded by me -- it basically tells me that everything is one and the same.
Nothing is different from I, because the I pervades everywhere. There is no space left. If you say I pervades only in sentient beings, then it is a different story.
But this I pervades everywhere. Aham Atma guda kesa sarva asyas thetah. Im seated in the hearts of all beings.
Im the core of all beings and things. So we have learnt and have an intellectual appreciation. Now, the knowledge in our life comes from three different sources.
One is Pratyaksa Pramana. You can keep telling me that it is night outside. You are hallucinating where I personally can see.
Thats the Pratyaksha Parama. I infer where there is smoke, there is fire. So chapter 10 gave me all the inferences.
How can I claim that there is electricity in this room? I said, dont you see the lights are on? That means electricity is on. Its an inference -- it does not say that I can see electricity. All my knowledge about electricity comes from inferences: the heater is on, lights are on, air conditioning is working.
But my Pratyaksha Pramana will be when I put my finger in that outlet. No words are necessary. No description is necessary.
Thats Pratyaksha Pramana -- seeing is the closest I can come. So our Shastra, the Sankhya philosophy, accepts three sources of knowledge. First, Pratyaksha Pramana -- perception through my senses.
Second, inference -- from my observation, I deduce that this must be the truth. And third is testimony -- somebody comes and tells me what it is. Most of our knowledge about Bhagavan comes from testimony only, so far.
My parents told me Bhagavan is like that. All religions tell me Bhagavan is all-pervading. Bhagavan is all-pervading.
Who am I to doubt him? So Im relying totally on testimony right now about Bhagavan, from a lineage of all the gurus. They are telling us that the Atma is the Paramatma. Who am I to question them? I have complete faith in them, in the testimony.
How does a judge ever decide what is right and what is wrong? Who is guilty, not guilty. He relies strictly on testimony, because he is hardly ever there at the scene of crime. Only in some very unique case does he happen to be there.
Otherwise, he never has any other means of knowledge other than testimony. Thats why the oath is taken: truth and nothing but the truth. So I can rely on testimony if I trust the testimony.
So far we have trusted the testimony of Bhagavan. Aham Atma Guda Kesas Sarva -- that is his testimony. He says so, and unless we doubt him, we dont have any reason to doubt him.
So we say okay, thats fine. Then he said, If you dont believe me just on my word, look everywhere around you and see all this power and glory. That power and glory will not be there if I am not there. So anytime I see something splendid.
Anytime you go out into nature, something awesome strikes you. Right away you have that sense of awe about the divine in nature. How wonderful this nature is! Because this exists, there must be God.
Because nature has laws, there must be a lawgiver. And because the laws are implicitly followed, there must be a law enforcer. We have never met him.
But we know if I jump from the 14th floor window, Mother Earth will receive me. As Newton figured out. But thats still not good enough for me to vouch for his presence.
What I want is seeing is believing. So Vishwarupadarshan is the final experience all of us are seeking. In spite of my complete faith in Bhagavad Gita and the teaching tradition, the only time I can come and tell you Bhagavan exists is if I experience him.
Therefore, now Arjuna says Mat Anugrahaa Paramam Guhiyam Adhyatma Sangin Matanughaya Paramam. Out of your great compassion for me -- not that I was deserving, not that I did something special. A mother does something for a child not because the child is deserving, but out of complete compassion.
Yat Paya Uktam -- out of great compassion for me, you have given me this secret knowledge about the self. You told me about what the Self is all about. In chapter two you told me that you are not that mortal being.
You are the immortal being. All beings are immortal. The self in them is immortal.
All bodies are destroyable, perishable. But the self in those bodies is immortal. You told me this great secret, which can only be transmitted when there is a great teacher and a very eligible student.
Otherwise the secret remains secret. Teachers may come and tell you, but you will never learn. My delusion is gone by this discourse.
This knowledge that you have given me out of your great compassion for me. So that confusion about who I am and what my duty is -- am I a soldier, a general? Or am I a brother, a grandson, and a student? What is more important, my duty as a general or my duty as a family man? That delusion is gone. The field of action changes, but I, the actor, remain the same.
So depending on the field of action, I should be working accordingly. I can think about architecture when that is my field. I cant start giving clients a discourse about Bhagavad Gita -- they will go away! The delusion is gone.
I now know what is right and what is wrong. However, Bhava Apyayo hi Bhutanam Srutao Vistara Shomaya. Let me also tell you what I understood so far.
That Bhava Apya origin and dissolution of beings in Bhutanam Sruta Vistara Somaya. I heard in detail which you told me Kamala Patraaksa Mahatmyam Apicha Avyam that it is the eternal self which is the origin and dissolution. Ishvara the Lord is the resting place and the source of all the beings.
Also Mahatmyam Apicha Abhyam. Then also your great glories. Then I heard you the Isvara.
I heard Your glories. He addresses Krishna Kamalapatra as one who is lotus eyed. Now obviously in our culture lotus eyed is considered beautiful.
But there is another implication here. That you are seeing this world as a lotus eyed. In other words, the lotus remains pure no matter what the condition of its being.
You the self remain unattached to all this prakriti that you have in detail described to me how this world functions. But you remain completely detached of that. I understood that part also.
I understood who I am, what my duty is. Now I also understood your nature as the Ishwara and how you remain detached from all the workings of this Prakriti. Evam etad yatha ATH tvam atmanam parameshwara.
Thus you have described Eva metat. So be it or so it is. Evam eta yatha atma as you said what we just discussed that you are the source of all the beings and you are the dissolution of all the beings.
That includes myself as well. You describe to me that you are the source of all the beings. You are the dissolution of all the beings.
However, Drastu mitchami -- I want to see it. I understood. There is no question anymore about the teaching.
However, I want to see it for myself. The sense of sight is the most dear to us, because seeing is believing. I may close my eyes and I may hear my granddaughter.
But that doesnt mean that she is here. Somebody put recording. I want to see what Im hearing is correct or something else Im hearing.
Thats why I want to have the direct experience. Only then can I vouch for it that your nature is such. I am understanding and accepting, with no doubt, the testimony you have given.
And all of this -- including Narad Muni, Kavi Ushna, and all the people we have talked about -- is testimony Ive taken for granted. As for inference, you told me to see everywhere in this world as you. I also understood that.
But I still need my direct experience. Pratyaksha Pramana. Drastumi Chami Terupam Ayeshwaram -- I want to see that splendid form of yours where everything is included in it.
Right now I only have a very narrow perspective. When we look at photographs of any building, we are only seeing a part of it.

Arjuna declares that his delusion is gone after hearing Krishnas teachings, yet he still yearns to see the cosmic form directly. This reveals a profound truth about spiritual growth: intellectual understanding, while necessary, is not the same as direct experience. Consider the three sources of knowledge mentioned in these verses - perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana), and testimony (shabda). Most of our spiritual knowledge comes from testimony - what teachers, scriptures, and traditions tell us. But like Arjuna, we long for that direct perception, that moment when seeing is believing.
Reflect today on the gap between what you intellectually know and what you have actually experienced. You may understand that all beings share the same consciousness, but do you feel it when interacting with a difficult colleague or a stranger on the street? Arjunas honesty is instructive - he does not pretend to have realized what he has only understood conceptually. Practice this honesty with yourself: Where in your spiritual journey are you relying purely on faith and testimony? What would it mean to move from hearing about the unity of existence to actually perceiving it?
As a daily exercise, when you encounter any moment of excellence or beauty today - a sunset, a kind gesture, a moment of insight - pause and ask yourself: Am I merely inferring the divine here, or can I directly perceive the source behind this manifestation? Let this question bridge the gap between knowledge heard and wisdom realized.
